unit.name: Investigating Small Business
unit.subtitle: How small businesses start, plan and respond to the world around them

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat cash flow and profit as the same thing, then conclude a profitable business cannot fail. They need to see a profitable firm running out of cash because of credit terms or stock build-up.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support guidance, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students compute break-even but cannot interpret what a change in fixed cost or selling price does to the diagram, so lose application marks on context-based extended responses.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support guidance, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name the case-study business in their first sentence and assume that counts as application. Pearson is explicit that the business name alone does not earn AO2 — students must embed specific scenario details such as product, location or numerical data.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support page, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse limited liability with limited responsibility, or think a sole trader's business assets are protected from creditors. Mistakes are common when sole trader/Ltd is the focus of a 6-mark Explain.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business chief examiner reports, June 2022 and June 2023, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list stakeholders without showing how interests collide (e.g. shareholder profit vs employee pay). Examiners want explicit conflict, not parallel descriptions.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business chief examiner reports, June 2023, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students forget to subtract the original investment when calculating average annual profit, or divide by the wrong number of years. ARR is one of the highest-error calculations in the Theme 2 quantitative skill set.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business chief examiner reports, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat globalisation as only a threat (cheap imports) without recognising the opportunities (overseas markets, lower input costs). One-sided answers lose marks on 9-mark Discuss responses.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business chief examiner reports, June 2023, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the four Ps as separate boxes rather than an integrated mix. Higher-mark answers show how a change in product forces a change in price, place or promotion.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support page, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate: Students show the formula and forget the numerical answer, or miss the units (£, %). Only the final answer is credited; formula statements earn zero. Two decimal places must be observed when specified. Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support, qualifications.pearson.com.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Calculate: Working is accepted but the boxed final answer is what scores. Students who place the answer outside the answer space or change units mid-calculation lose marks even with correct method. Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Explain: Students drift into a third or fourth point. Pearson examiners only mark the best two — the safest tactic is two well-developed points, each making a statement of fact plus two expansion points that link logically. No context is required (and adding it does not earn extra marks here). Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Discuss: Generic answers with no reference to the case-study context stall around the middle of the rubric (Developing). Students must integrate at least two contextual details — specific product, customer base, location, financial figures — into substantive analytical points to reach Secure or Mastering. Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Justify a Recommendation: Candidates need not address both options — a fully developed single option with pros, cons and a contextualised conclusion can reach the Mastering tier. Students who simply list both options in parallel without judgement stall in Developing. Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate a Statement: The conclusion must add new evaluative thinking, not summarise prior points. Phrases like 'it depends' without supporting criteria do not earn evaluation marks. Examiners apply a best-fit judgement across knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation strands. Source: Pearson GCSE Business Assessment Support.

topic_weighting_notes: Both themes are 90 marks each and weighted equally (50/50). Theme 1 lessons should not eclipse Theme 2 — plan to ~15 lessons each.

Quantitative skills are worth ~10% of the total qualification (around 18 marks across the qualification). Calculations are spread across topics 1.3, 2.4 and embedded elsewhere — break-even, cash flow and ARR are the high-frequency calculations.

Each theme paper opens with a stand-alone block (~35 marks of MCQ, short-answer and small calculation, no source booklet) and is followed by two longer blocks (~55 marks total) of extended responses tied to a separate source booklet context. Plan exam tips and practice questions to reflect both modes.
AO weighting across the qualification: AO1 ~35%, AO2 ~35%, AO3 ~30%. AO2 application is the single most discriminating skill — over a third of marks require contextualisation.
Topic 1.5 (external influences) is heavily synoptic — students are expected to draw on it across both themes.
Topic 2.1.4 (ethics and environment) is increasingly prominent in 12-mark extended-evaluation questions — Pearson has signalled this in recent assessment-support webinars.
current_spec_changes: Specification Issue 2 (July 2022) extended both paper timings from 1h30 to 1h45. Source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Business Specification Issue 2 (July 2022), qualifications.pearson.com.

Specification Issue 2 confirmed that questions in Sections B and C are now based on contexts given in a separate Source Booklet rather than printed inside the paper. Source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Business Specification Issue 2 (July 2022).
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance on Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools recommends explicit teaching of disciplinary writing — modelling how an Analyse or Evaluate response is structured, not just telling students to 'write more'. Build this into every extended-writing exam tip. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk, Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.

EEF Maths in Context evaluation suggests financial-context calculations (cash flow, break-even) are where students most often fail to transfer numeracy — embed real worked examples rather than abstract formula drills. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk, Maths in Context project.

Cambridge Assessment research on extended-response marking shows that levels-based mark schemes have the lowest examiner agreement of any format — students benefit from seeing exemplar paragraphs at each rubric tier (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging) rather than trying to infer level boundaries. Source: cambridgeassessment.org.uk, Macinska & Benton (2020), 'The usefulness of detailed marks within levels-based mark schemes'.

Tes practitioner consensus on GCSE Business: case-study habit-building works best when application is taught as a skill (annotate the source, then write) rather than as a sentence-starter. Build annotate-first prompts into the practice questions for context-based extended-response items. Source: tes.com, GCSE Business case-study and exam-skills resources (style/structure reference only).
